Amine. A functional group and class of organic compounds containing a basic nitrogen atom with a lone pair. Amines are structurally derived from ammonia, where one or more hydrogen atoms are replaced with alkyl or aryl groups. Like ammonia, amines are weak bases and nucleophiles, playing a vital role in biochemistry as components of amino acids, neurotransmitters like dopamine, and alkaloids.

Amines are classified as primary, secondary, tertiary, or quaternary depending on how many carbon groups are bonded directly to the nitrogen atom. Quaternary ammonium ions carry a permanent positive charge. They're known for intense, foul odors resembling rotting fish or decaying flesh. The simple diamines putrescine and cadaverine are notorious examples.

Amines can be synthesized cleanly via the Gabriel synthesis, which uses potassium phthalimide and an alkyl halide to produce primary amines while avoiding the over-alkylation that commonly occurs with direct amine alkylation. They undergo Hofmann elimination, where an amine is treated with excess methyl iodide and silver oxide, then heated, to yield the least substituted alkene. Amines can also be produced via the Hofmann rearrangement, which degrades a primary amide to an amine with one fewer carbon atom using bromine and a strong base.

The lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom determines both the basicity and nucleophilicity of the amine. When an amine condenses with a carboxylic acid or its derivatives, it yields an amide. Amino acids are organic molecules that serve as the monomers of proteins, and they're characterized by having both an amine group and a carboxylic acid group.
